closing.items_title: Every build of the night, oldest first

closing.title: What got better and what did not, in my honest view

columns.title: Better
items: The screen is calm. Every kind of thing has one fixed place: the ledger top left, the shop top right, the bell bottom left, navigation bottom right, one message top centre, one line of guidance bottom centre. A check compares every state of the screen on eight window and interface sizes with the layout sheet: nothing overlaps, nothing is cut off, nothing changes place when something else appears.

The shop is a list of rows with a price instead of twelve three-line cards. Locked purchases are named on their group's heading, finished ones leave, each row has its own icon, and a tooltip says what a purchase does, what it is worth and why it cannot be bought yet. Eighteen text sizes became four.

Messages wait their turn. One banner at a time, one note at a time, none appearing in a single frame; about two thirds of the old notes are gone; a banner that is no longer true is dropped; a request says Done or Too late in its own place.
The first minute explains itself with four short hints that show once.

The town is better to look at: villagers are people with hats, hoods and arms; cottages come in nine shapes with chimneys and smoke; a real mill whose sails turn; five kinds of tree; fields that read as crops; a river with banks, reeds and shimmer; crossings and boats that can be read; the charter stone found at a glance.
The book lies on a wooden table and has tooled leather; its turning leaf looks like a leaf; an interrupted animation keeps its speed; the pause question and the settings' boxes are one kind of card.

How it plays is unchanged by the numbers: the whole first age played through real clicks and keys reaches the charter at minute 33.9 with 201 purchases, with the same purchases and decisions a minute as before the night.

columns.title: Not better
items: Nobody has played this with their own hands or heard any of its sounds. Everything was judged from pictures, twelve-frame strips and measurements, on a machine without a graphics card.

The second age was not played through by real input, as your step 6 asked "if there is time left": there was none. Villagers housed by the river still walk home to a first-age cottage, and the ford still matters on about half of the towns.
There is no title page when the game starts.
The animals are too small to see at the normal view; a reviewer wrote "the town is not yet alive". Loads are a few pixels there too and read by colour more than by shape.
The gable-ended cottage reads dark from above, and every roof is the same thatch yellow.
With many things affordable the shop is a wall of gold pills, and early in the game the ledger is mostly blank ruled paper.
The age-change leaf reads as a leaf laid down and lifted again, not as one forward turn. Pressing Esc twice quickly still overshoots a little.
Zoomed out, the page stage and the book stage now look almost alike: both show the whole book.

In pave mode two labels show near the pointer at once (the suggested price and the road's own price), and the milestone note in the ledger is set in a heavier letter than everything around it. Both were found in the last pictures, too late to fix.
In the second age the shop fills the whole right side from top to bottom once the river group opens, and villagers pile up in one dark knot at the landing.
At interface size 150 percent the ledger's "Next:" line is shortened with three dots, and the shop rows lose their second line (what a purchase is worth); the tooltip still says it.
The digits have a slashed zero (the interface font has no other); it reads as code in a book.
The small rewards (the coin hop, dust, ripples, the bell's rings) were reviewed once and fixed once; I have not seen them move.

Under load three tests are not steady (a row coming to rest in the town test, a ten-second wait in the settings test, the motion test's 6 ms gate): they pass on a quiet machine, but a steady test would not need one.

closing.title: Decisions made for you
head: Decision
Why
rows: The interface and the assets are worked on at the same time, in two checkouts, and merged after each round
The night is ten hours; the brief asks for a third of it on the layout and a quarter on assets. Their files do not overlap
Last night's log moved to docs/incremental-log-night2.md; this file starts fresh
One file to resume from, short enough to read after a restart
The before pictures are kept in git as JPEG (docs/review/n3/before/)
The review page must show before and after even if the cloud machine is replaced in the night
The left side of the screen becomes one "ledger" sheet that never changes size, with four ruled sections (purse, goal, a strip, a note); an empty section shows blank ruled paper
Four separate cards that came and went were a main cause of the chaos; a fixed sheet means nothing can move or pop in
The shop becomes rows in one sheet: name and what it is worth on the left, a price pill on the right; locked purchases are named on the group's heading ("Yoke at level 7") instead of having rows
Calmer than twelve three-line cards, and nothing a player could read before is lost
About two thirds of the small notes are no longer shown ("A cottage is extended", "A road is cobbled", "A new villager moves in", "New to buy", "A road has worn in", a request asked, met or missed)
They said what the player had just done or what another part of the screen already shows. A first age had about 200 notes, six a minute
"Ring in the next age" lives in the ledger's strip, as a gold button that stays until used
It had no fixed place; it is the most important button of the age
Coin numbers on the map are smaller (20 instead of 34) and stay 1.4 s instead of 1.8 s
They covered villagers and labels. The setting that turns them off stays
A purchase's step is shown as a plain number after its name ("Villager 9") instead of "level 9"
"Level" also means the town's level, a few centimetres away
The 150 percent interface size is honoured on a 1280 x 720 window too (the shop then uses one-line rows and may scroll)
The brief asks for it; a critic proposed capping it instead
Fields are reworked although they are not on your list
In the audit they read as pallets of planks, and they are the largest things on the map
No new keys are added (river purchases stay without keys; the choice of two keeps Z and X)
Adding keys would change how the game is played
Building offers take the keys F, G and H in the order of the rows you can see
Locked offers are no longer rows, so the first visible offer is always F. Before, a locked offer could hold F
A request's bar shows how much is delivered, not how much time is left; the time is in the text and turns red in its last quarter
A reviewer found that a request that was nearly met looked like a failing one
At a level with a choice of two boons, the choice opens at once and the level's gift is told in a note
The sheet first said "banner first"; a decision should not be held back for three seconds
Labels on the map (a staked plot, a boat's cargo, "+ hand") are small paper tags at a fixed size on screen
The old 3D labels shrank to 5 to 7 pixels at 1280 x 720
Cottage variant and door colour follow from a cottage's place in the town, not from the save
The save format does not change, and the same town always looks the same
The book's table now has an inkwell and quill, a candle, a ribbon and a seal stamp lying at its edges
The table was a flat dark brown filling 40 percent of the book view
A ferryman, a boatman and a skipper stand on the raft and in the boats (decoration only)
The ferry and the boats looked abandoned
The book's work ran in a third checkout beside the message round, with file ownership split between them
To leave time for the feel round and the final checks
About two thirds of the small notes are gone, and a banner is dropped when it is no longer true (a level banner once the town has passed that level)
Late news is noise
The four first-minute hints are remembered in the settings file, so a new town does not show them again
"Never again" in your brief; the save format stays as it is
The step "if there is time left" (the second age played by real input; a title page) is not started unless the last-look list is done by 03:50
The layout, the messages and the assets took the night, as the brief ranks them
The small rewards are thinned when the town is busy (some are skipped, none queue)
Your brief: keep them light; with thirty villagers every delivery would otherwise flicker
Each cottage size has its own scale again (0.86, 0.91, 0.95 of its plot)
The first asset round had made plain cottages smaller than they were before the night
Zoomed out, the page stage now shows the whole book inside the window (it used to show the map's page with its edges cut)
Reviewers found the compass and the page number cut off; the side effect is that the page and book stages look alike
The age-change page turn is a leaf with the new age's title on it, above the whole interface
It was a paper sweep with the shop drawn over it
Achievement medals are shown on the achievements page and in achievement notes; other message kinds have icons drawn but not yet shown
Time; the layout check had to pass with every change

closing.title: Needs you
items: Play the newest Windows build yourself. Everything tonight was judged from pictures and measurements on a machine without a graphics card: say whether the screen stays calm in play, whether messages come at a good pace, and whether anything stutters.
Listen. The six new reward sounds have players on the review page; in the game, check that a sound now comes with its message and that the sounds do not pile up when the town is busy.
Answer the yes-or-no questions on the review page and say continue.

Decide about the digits. The interface font draws a slashed zero and has no other; plain zeros need another font for numbers (a free-licence font from a site this machine may not reach, which needs your approval) or digits drawn by us.

Say whether the next round should go to what was not reached tonight: the second age played through by real input (river villagers walking home to first-age cottages, the ford mattering on half the towns) and a title page.

closing.title: New sounds to listen to
paras: Made in code tonight and checked only by measurement: nobody has heard them.

tunes.title: Coin hop
tunes.note: a small coin flicked up and landing on others, 0.4 s, four variants. Plays as a delivery's coin lands, at most every 0.3 s.

tunes.title: Dust puff
tunes.note: a breath of dry earth with a few grains, 0.35 s, three variants. Plays when a cottage is extended and, quieter, for dust on a new trail.

tunes.title: Grit
tunes.note: a handful of gravel scattering, 0.55 s, three variants. Plays when a road is paved.

tunes.title: Ripple
tunes.note: a small lap of water and a bubble, 0.5 s, three variants. Plays when a boat moors or casts off, when goods are sold at the landing and at the ford's stones.

tunes.title: Bell creak
tunes.note: the bell's yoke turning in its wooden frame, 0.45 s, two variants. Plays with the bell and with each peal of the new age.

tunes.title: Gift ring
tunes.note: a soft struck chime, 0.9 s, two notes. Plays when a level's gift arrives and at a purchase that has a place on the map.
